prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, reaching fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: After reading the full set of opening ballots I move my preferred configuration from my own first choice (B005, active matter) to the optical lattice clock. I ranked it only sixth, mainly because it lies outside my own field, but the colleagues who know precision measurement best make a case I find persuasive on the criteria that matter. The idea is simple and general (a magic wavelength makes the lattice light shift cancel, so many atoms can be interrogated in a Doppler- and recoil-free regime). It was a clear invention rather than an incremental improvement, and it has been realised and surpassed by independent groups at JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others, with mutually consistent international comparisons. It also yields real physics: tests of constant drift, relativistic redshift over millimetres, and a concrete route to redefining the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: all eight members independently proposed exactly Katori and Ye, which at least shows that the credited names are not contested. I value a result I can state as one mechanism and verify against experiment, and this is that kind of result.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the frequency comb (Hall and Haensch, 2005) and ion-trap clocks (Wineland, 2012) already recognised adjacent parts of the precision-timekeeping chain, so the committee must be able to argue that the lattice clock is a distinct, conceptual step and not merely better engineering of an already honoured field. There is also a credit question about other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom) whose contributions sit beside Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy records. Finally, a prize that is widely expected can crowd out candidates that are less well known to the committee but have equal scientific weight. I note that my own preferred field, B005, has the opposite problem: strong ideas and good experiments, but narrower committee familiarity.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranks B009 first as precision atomic physics at its best: a clear, original idea, confirmed by many laboratories, with a clean two-person credit and timely maturity.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of this argument and it has changed my ranking. What persuades me is not the fame of the clock but the cancellation mechanism, the independent replication, and the fact that clock comparisons give consistency checks that few fields can match. I would press one point further than you did. The case for a distinct step beyond the 2005 comb prize should be made explicitly in the citation, so I would anchor it on magic-wavelength trapping and not on 'optical clocks' in general.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranks B009 first as a textbook case of a technique that moved the limit of what can be measured, with Katori's proposal and Ye's group performance as a clear two-person pair, and he ranks B001 (atom interferometry) third.
responses.response: I agree on B009 and on the clean pairing. I am less convinced by B001 for this year. The credit there is visibly incomplete, since you yourself note that Chu is missing from the list and Wallraff-type omissions are the sort of problem a committee cannot repair at the last minute, and the most compelling applications are still maturing. A prize is easier to defend where the credited names carry the discovery completely, which B009 does and B001 does not.

responses.point: Goran Johansson puts B008 (circuit QED) first and B009 second, arguing that circuit QED is mature, confirmed in many labs over about twenty years, and timely after the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I take the scientific case for circuit QED seriously, but I disagree on its priority. Eriksson's and Danielsson's ballots both note that Wallraff is absent from the credited list, so the three names as supplied omit someone who made the first strong-coupling experiment. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is also close enough that I would worry about giving the same platform a second prize so soon. I would keep B008 as a strong later candidate and not the pick for this year.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson ranks B018 (topological insulators) first and B019 (magic-angle graphene) second, citing the rare combination of theoretical prediction followed by experimental realisation in HgTe.
responses.response: Prediction followed by realisation is a legitimate criterion and B018 satisfies it. I ranked B018 last of my list, though, for two reasons you do not weigh heavily: the 2016 prize recognised topological phases, so the overlap is real, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are missing from the credit, which means the realisation in HgTe followed a proposal that the prize would leave out. On B019, I share your enthusiasm but only about eight years have passed and the pairing mechanism is unsettled, so I would let that one mature.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson ranks B050 (CMB anisotropies) first as the logical successor to the 2006 COBE prize, and notes the allocation problem created by the Planck and WMAP collaborations.
responses.response: I accept that the CMB measurements are among the most consequential in cosmology and that the results have been confirmed by Planck, ACT and SPT. My difficulty is the same attribution problem you raise: a WMAP trio omits Planck leadership, and an additional name from Planck would push the credit past three. The shortlist offers a candidate whose credited names carry the whole result, so I would choose that first and treat B050 as a case that needs a better credit solution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as a distinct conceptual step beyond the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or as an extension of an already honoured field.
Whether other lattice-clock contributors (for example Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom) are important enough to complicate the two-person credit.
I am not a specialist in precision atomic physics and rely on colleagues' reading of the clock-comparison literature.
The active-matter case (B005) has only my own support in this round, so I cannot tell how it would be judged by colleagues who know the field less well.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates: none of Katori, Ye, Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Toner, Ramaswamy or Vicsek appears among my frequent co-authors. I note only that I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), which is an institutional fact, not a conflict about any candidate; I do not work in the optical-clock or active-matter groups.
